summary: Defines a MIB for managed objects that model the Link Management Protocol. It provides minor corrections to and obsoletes RFC 4327. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a set of gauges for a protocol that checks the links between network devices.

subtitle: The SNMP management objects for configuring and monitoring the Link Management Protocol on optical and routing gear.

tldr.problem: The Link Management Protocol (LMP) keeps control channels alive, checks data-bearing links and isolates link faults, but operators need a standard way to configure it and read its counters from a management system.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4631 defines LMP-MIB, an SNMP MIB module with tables for neighbors, control channels, TE links, link verification and data-bearing links, plus performance counters and eight notifications.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track document that obsoletes RFC 4327 with minor corrections, chiefly making TruthValue descriptions consistent (True is 1, False is 2).

today: RFC 4631 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4327. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the LMP MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4631 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols, in particular for modeling the Link Management Protocol (LMP) defined in RFC 4204. MIB objects are generally reached through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and the module is written in SMIv2.

The text places LMP alongside Generalized MPLS (GMPLS). The primary purpose of LMP is to manage traffic engineering (TE) links. Its main goals are keeping control channel connectivity up, correlating link properties, verifying data-bearing links, and detecting and isolating link faults.

The MIB module covers both configuration and performance monitoring. It is meant to work hand in hand with the TE Link MIB of RFC 4220, which holds the table that ties data-bearing links to TE links.
sections.plainLanguage: LMP is a way for two machines to check that the wires between them work. This document is the shared list of settings and counters a person can use to control and watch that checking.

sections.title: Adjacencies, Control Channels and TE Links
sections.content:
An LMP adjacency is formed between two nodes that support the same capabilities. LMP messages travel between the pair over control channels, and several control channels can be active at the same time. Apart from control channel management messages, an LMP message for a neighbor can be sent on any active control channel. Control channels can also carry MPLS control plane or routing information.

LMP supports aggregating one or more data-bearing links into a traffic-engineering (TE) link. Data-bearing links are either component links or ports, depending on their multiplexing capability. Each TE link is associated with one LMP adjacency, and the control channels of that adjacency are used to manage the TE links.

The MIB is designed to enable and disable LMP on LMP-capable interfaces of a photonic switch, optical cross-connect or router, to report on adjacencies, to configure keep-alive and link verification parameters, to map local and remote TE links and interface identifiers, and to provide performance counters per control channel and per data-bearing link.
sections.plainLanguage: Two neighbors talk over one or more phone lines (control channels). Their job is to look after the real roads (data links) bundled together into one big highway (a TE link).

sections.title: The Tables in the Module
sections.content:
The module is organised as eight tables. Each configuration table has rows that are created and removed with a RowStatus object and carries a StorageType object, which defaults to nonVolatile.

  • lmpNbrTable identifies the pair of nodes that exchange LMP messages. It also holds retransmission settings: an initial retransmit interval (default 500), a retry limit (default 3, where 0 means never stop retransmitting) and a delta that controls exponential backoff. These implement the congestion-handling mechanism of RFC 4204, which is based on RFC 2914.
  • lmpControlChannelTable enables LMP on LMP-capable interfaces. A device creates an entry for every LMP-capable interface.
  • lmpControlChannelPerfTable holds per-control-channel counters, one entry for each control channel entry.
  • lmpTeLinkTable holds LMP information specific to TE links.
  • lmpLinkVerificationTable configures link verification for each TE link that supports the procedure.
  • lmpTeLinkPerfTable holds per-TE-link counters.
  • lmpDataLinkTable lists the data-bearing links associated with TE links.
  • lmpDataLinkPerfTable holds counters for data-bearing links.

There are also node-wide scalars, for example lmpAdminStatus and lmpOperStatus, and defaults for the Hello keep-alive intervals. The Hello dead interval should be at least three times the Hello interval. The counters count LMP messages such as Config, Hello, BeginVerify, EndVerify, TestStatus, LinkSummary and ChannelStatus, sent, received and retransmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is like a filing cabinet with eight drawers. Each drawer holds the settings or the scoreboard for one part of the link-checking job.

sections.title: Worked Example: Setting Up a Control Channel
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an example with two control channels between two nodes and three data-bearing links. The data-bearing links are ports (lambdas).

The order of rows matters. First a row goes into lmpNbrTable with the neighbor's node ID. Then the two control channels are created in lmpControlChannelTable, each with Hello interval 15 and Hello dead interval 45. Next the three data-bearing links are created in lmpDataLinkTable; an interface entry with the same ifIndex must exist beforehand. Then a TE link is created as an interface of type teLink in the ifTable, and a matching row goes into lmpTeLinkTable and lmpLinkVerificationTable.

The data-bearing link type does not need to be provisioned because the node fills it in automatically. The association between data-bearing links and the TE link is stored in the ifStackTable of the Interfaces Group MIB. The RFC says the example is not meant to show every nuance of the module.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting it up is like building a toy railway in order: first say who the neighbor is, then lay the two phone lines, then add the three tracks, and finally tie them into one named route.

sections.title: Interfaces Group and Notifications
sections.content:
A control channel may be modeled as an interface in the Interfaces Group MIB (RFC 2863). This is signalled by lmpCcIsIf being true (1). In that case the channel SHOULD appear as an ifEntry with ifType 227 (lmp), stacked over whatever interface it transmits on. If the underlying layer offers multiple access, several LMP interfaces can be stacked on it in parallel. Modeling control channels as interfaces is not a requirement: when lmpCcIsIf is false (2) there is simply no ifTable entry.

The module also defines eight notifications: TE link property mismatch, data link property mismatch, unprotected (the last redundant control channel failed), control channel up, control channel down, TE link degraded, TE link no longer degraded, and data link verification failure. Each is off unless its enable object is set, and all enable objects default to false. Because verification failures can repeat, a data link verification notification can occur no more than once per data link per verification interval, and lmpNotificationMaxRate can throttle notifications to a maximum per minute, where 0 means no throttling.
sections.plainLanguage: Each phone line can get its own entry on the building's equipment list, or not, whichever you like. The panel can also ring a bell when something changes, but only if you switch the bell on, and you can limit how often it rings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access may be sensitive. Unauthorized changes to lmpNbrTable, lmpControlChannelTable, lmpTeLinkTable and lmpDataLinkTable may disrupt allocation of resources in the network.

Readable objects can also be sensitive. lmpNbrTable exposes the provider's node IP addresses, lmpControlChannelTable exposes its control network, and lmpDataLinkTable exposes its data network.

The RFC states that SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security and that deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. It RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with cryptographic security, and makes it the operator's responsibility to give access only to principals with a legitimate right to read or change the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The control panel shows secrets about how the network is built, and a wrong twist of a dial could break things. So only trusted people should get the key, and the key should be a strong one.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4327
sections.content:
RFC 4631 provides minor corrections to and obsoletes RFC 4327. The key technical fix is that TruthValue settings are now described consistently, with True always 1 and False always 2. Other listed changes add punctuation to REFERENCE clauses, remove square braces from references inside the module, update the revision history, timestamps, author information and acknowledgements, and make editorial corrections.

There are no new IANA actions. The earlier assignments still hold: ifType 227 for LMP interfaces, and { transmission 227 } for the LMP-MIB module. The module's revision history shows 14 August 2006 for this revision and 11 January 2006 for RFC 4327.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of the dial list. It fixes small mistakes, like two places that disagreed about whether yes is 1 or 2, so every maker reads it the same way.
